title: The Infinitive and its Uses
summary: The infinitive of ¶40 was only a complement after *galėti* and *norėti*. It also names purpose after a verb of motion, stands as a subject like a noun, and completes the impersonals already met — three jobs that must not be confused.

rules.heading: The Complementary Infinitive Extended
rules.statement: ¶40 gave the infinitive after **galėti**, **norėti** and **mėgti**. The same construction completes a much longer list of verbs that need a second action rather than a noun: **pradėti** (to begin), **baigti** (to finish), **turėti** in the sense *to have to*, **bandyti** (to try), **mokėti** (to know how), **norėti** and **galėti** as before. The finite verb alone carries person and tense; the infinitive never changes.

paradigms.caption: Finite verb + infinitive
paradigms.footnote: *Turėti* with a noun still means *to have* (*turiu knygą*); with an infinitive it means *must / have to*. The complement decides the sense.

examples.gloss: Can you swim? (do you know how)

rules.heading: The Purposive Infinitive after Motion
rules.statement: After a verb of **motion** — *eiti, važiuoti, ateiti, eiti namo* and their kin — an infinitive states the **purpose** of the going: *einu pirkti* is *I am going (in order) to buy*. English often inserts *to* or *in order to*; Lithuanian puts the bare infinitive next to the motion verb. No *kad* is needed for this short construction.

examples.gloss: I am going to buy bread.
examples.note: genitive after a verb of obtaining, as at ¶32

examples.gloss: We are going to Vilnius to study.

footnotes: The motion verb is finite and carries the tense; the infinitive only names the purpose. *Einu pirkti* is present going; *ėjau pirkti* was past going for that purpose.

rules.heading: Purpose with Kad and the Conditional
rules.statement: When the purpose is a full clause — especially when its subject differs, or when no motion verb is present — Lithuanian uses **kad** with the **conditional**: *Dirbu, kad uždirbčiau* — I work so that I may earn. The conditional here is not politeness (¶112) but the mood of a purpose not yet achieved. **Tam, kad** makes the purpose explicit when the clause is heavy.

examples.gloss: I study so that I can speak Lithuanian.

examples.target: Jis dirba, kad šeima gyventų geriau.
examples.gloss: He works so that the family may live better.
Come earlier so that we may manage in time.

footnotes: Do not use a bare infinitive for this: *Dirbu uždirbti* is not Lithuanian. Motion + infinitive (¶176) is one construction; *kad* + conditional is the other.

rules.heading: The Nominal Infinitive
rules.statement: An infinitive may stand as the **subject** (or predicative complement) of a sentence, naming the action as a thing is named. The predicate is then usually a **neuter** adjective of the kind met at ¶121 — *gera, sunku, naudinga, brangu* — which agrees with nothing, because the subject is not a gendered noun. English often uses a gerund (*reading is useful*); Lithuanian keeps the infinitive.

examples.target: Mokytis lietuvių kalbos sunku, bet įdomu.
examples.gloss: Learning Lithuanian is hard but interesting.

rules.heading: The Infinitive Keeps its Own Government
rules.statement: Whatever case a verb governs as a finite form, it governs in the **infinitive** too. *Skaityti knygą* keeps the accusative; *norėti kavos* in a larger phrase still shows the genitive on the noun if *norėti* is the governing verb; *eiti į mokyklą* keeps *į* + accusative. The complementary or purposive frame does not rewrite the inner case.

examples.gloss: I want to read this book.
examples.note: *skaityti* takes accusative *knygą*; *norėti* here takes the infinitive, not a genitive noun

examples.gloss: I am going to buy milk.
examples.note: genitive after *pirkti* in the partitive sense

examples.gloss: We have to help a friend.

rules.heading: Choosing the Construction
rules.statement: Three questions decide the form. Is the infinitive completing a verb such as *galėti, norėti, pradėti*? → complementary (¶175). Is it the purpose of a verb of motion, with no new subject? → bare purposive infinitive (¶176). Is the purpose a full clause, often with a different subject? → *kad* + conditional (¶177). Is the action itself the subject of *yra sunku / naudinga*? → nominal infinitive (¶178). Mixing them — *einu, kad pirkti* or *dirbu uždirbti* — is the error this section exists to prevent.

rows.label: nominal
cells: *Skaitymas yra naudingas* is possible but a different style

examples.gloss: I begin to write so that I may finish today.

vocabulary.gloss: to know how; to be able (skill) (+ infinitive)
to rest, to have a rest

vocabulary.notes: Neuter predicate naudinga with a nominal infinitive.
Introduces a purpose clause; usually with the conditional.

vocabulary.gloss: to manage in time, to catch
to rest, to take a rest

drills.explanation: **Pradėti** takes a complementary infinitive: *pradedu mokytis*. The finite forms *mokausi / mokiausi* would make a second finite verb without a conjunction.

drills.stem: Complete: **Einu ____ duonos.** (I am going to buy bread.)
drills.explanation: Motion + purpose takes the bare infinitive **pirkti**. A second finite verb would need its own clause.
A nominal infinitive takes a **neuter** predicate: *naudinga*. The masculine *naudingas* would agree with a masculine noun, which the infinitive is not.
*Turėti* + infinitive is obligation — *have to*. Ability is *galiu eiti*; possession is *turiu* + a noun.

drills.stem: Which sentences correctly use a **purposive** infinitive after motion?
drills.explanation: The first, second and fourth follow a motion verb. *Dirbu uždirbti* wrongly uses a bare infinitive where purpose needs *kad* + conditional (¶177).
A purpose clause with **kad** takes the **conditional**: *galėčiau*. The indicative and the bare infinitive are the usual interference errors.
The governing verb for the noun is *skaityti*, which takes the accusative: **šią knygą**. *Norėti* here takes the infinitive, so it does not put the book into the genitive.

options: *Dirbu, kad uždirbčiau* uses the conditional of purpose.
*Turiu knygą* and *turiu eiti* use *turėti* in the same sense.
A nominal infinitive often takes a neuter adjective as predicate.
drills.explanation: *Turiu knygą* is possession; *turiu eiti* is obligation. The complement — noun against infinitive — decides the sense (¶175).

drills.stem: Which is the correct purpose clause?
drills.explanation: Without a motion verb, purpose is **kad** + conditional. A bare infinitive after *dirbti* is not available; *kad* + infinitive is equally wrong.

drills.stem: How many distinct **jobs** can the infinitive do at this level?
drills.explanation: Four: complement, purpose after motion, purpose with *kad* + conditional, and nominal subject. Mixing them is the usual error.

options: Because all purposive infinitives govern the genitive.
Because *pirkti* here takes the partitive genitive of what is obtained, as at A1.
drills.explanation: The infinitive keeps the government of its verb (¶179). *Pirkti* with an indefinite amount takes the genitive; *eiti* only supplies the motion.

drills.title: Kodėl Tomas mokosi?
drills.passage: Tomas nori mokytis lietuvių kalbos, nes gyventi Vilniuje be kalbos sunku. Kiekvieną rytą jis eina į biblioteką skaityti. Jis pradeda dirbti anksti, kad vakare galėtų pailsėti. Draugai sako: „Tu turi daugiau ilsėtis!“ Bet Tomas atsako: „Bandau baigti knygą šiandien. Skaityti man naudinga, o kalbėti lietuviškai — dar naudingiau. Važiuoju į kursus mokytis, ne tik klausyti.“ Jeigu spės, jis ateis padėti man pirkti dovaną.
drills.translation: Tomas wants to learn Lithuanian, because living in Vilnius without the language is hard. Every morning he goes to the library to read. He begins to work early so that in the evening he can rest. Friends say: "You have to rest more!" But Tomas answers: "I am trying to finish the book today. Reading is useful for me, and speaking Lithuanian is even more useful. I go to the courses to study, not only to listen." If he manages in time, he will come to help me buy a gift.

questions.stem: Why does Tomas want to learn Lithuanian?
options: Because living in Vilnius without the language is hard.
Because he must buy a gift today.
questions.explanation: *gyventi Vilniuje be kalbos sunku* — a nominal infinitive with the neuter predicate *sunku*, giving the reason after *nes*.
The first three follow *eiti / važiuoti / ateiti*. *Pradeda dirbti* is a complementary infinitive after *pradėti*, not purpose of motion.

questions.stem: **kad vakare galėtų pailsėti** — which construction is this?
questions.explanation: *Kad* + conditional *galėtų* is the purpose clause of ¶177, here completing why he begins work early.

options: Because the subject is an infinitive and the predicate is neuter.
questions.explanation: Nominal infinitive + neuter adjective (¶178, ¶121). *Man* is the person concerned (dative), not the subject that would force agreement.

questions.stem: How many complementary infinitives depend on **bandyti**, **pradėti**, or **turėti** in the passage?
questions.explanation: Three: *pradeda dirbti*, *turi … ilsėtis*, *Bandau baigti*. (*Nori mokytis* is also complementary, but after *norėti*, not one of the three verbs named in the question.)

drills.stem: Complete: **Bandau ____ lietuviškai.** (I try to speak Lithuanian.)
drills.explanation: **Bandyti** takes a complementary infinitive: *bandau kalbėti*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Ar moki ____?** (Can you swim? / do you know how)
drills.explanation: *Mokėti* (know how) + infinitive: *moki plaukti*.
Motion + bare purposive infinitive: *atėjo padėti*. No *kad* needed.
Nominal infinitive as subject with neuter *naudinga*: *Skaityti yra naudinga*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Dirbu, kad ____.** (I work so that I may earn.)
drills.explanation: Purpose with *kad* takes the **conditional**: *kad uždirbčiau*.
*Einu pirkti* is **purposive** after motion, not complementary. The others complete *pradėti / turėti / baigti*.

drills.stem: **Noriu skaityti šią knygą.** Who governs *šią knygą*?
options: the whole phrase as one case
drills.explanation: The infinitive keeps its own government: *skaityti* takes accusative *knygą*; *norėti* here takes the infinitive.
Bare infinitive purpose without motion is not Lithuanian: use *kad* + conditional, not *dirbu uždirbti*.

options: Dirbu, kad uždirbčiau — kad + conditional purpose
drills.explanation: *Skaityti naudinga* is the **nominal** infinitive, not a complement of *galėti*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Turime padėti ____.** (We have to help a friend.)
drills.explanation: *Padėti* keeps its **dative** under the infinitive: *padėti draugui*.

drills.stem: Which of these verbs take a **complementary** infinitive?
drills.explanation: *pradėti*, *bandyti*, and *mokėti* take a complementary infinitive. *eiti* takes a purposive infinitive of motion.

drills.stem: How many distinct **infinitive uses** must be kept apart at this level?
drills.explanation: Four: complementary, motion-purpose, *kad* + conditional purpose, and nominal.

drills.stem: **Turiu eiti** against **turiu knygą** — what decides the sense?
drills.explanation: Infinitive → *must / have to*; noun → *have*. The complement decides.
*Pradedu mokytis* is complementary (*pradėti* + infinitive), not motion purpose.
